removal_facts: You own the copyright to your own photos and videos; sites hosting them without permission are infringing.
A DMCA takedown notice is a formal request to a host or search engine to remove infringing content; most US-based hosts and Google honor valid notices.
Google can delist an infringing URL from search results even when the host is slow to remove it - these are two separate actions.
Removals typically take anywhere from 24 hours to a few weeks depending on the host and its jurisdiction.
Sending the notice to the site's hosting/registrar abuse contact is often more effective than the site's own form.
Keep evidence: the original post URL, the leak URL, and the date you found it, in case you need to escalate.
Many leak sites re-upload after removal, so ongoing monitoring plus repeat notices is normal.
You do not need to be a lawyer to file a DMCA notice, but it must be accurate and made in good faith.
Non-US hosts may not follow DMCA but usually respond to their local copyright or hosting-abuse process.
Delisting content from search sharply cuts its traffic even if a copy lingers on an obscure host.
You own the copyright automatically the moment you create a photo or video — no registration or lawyer is needed to send a takedown.
Content you posted to OnlyFans, Fansly or Instagram is still yours; a leak of it is copyright infringement.
Most leak sites hide their real host behind Cloudflare; Cloudflare won't remove content but WILL forward your report to the real host and tell you who it is.
If a leak is a non-consensual intimate image, you can use fast-track tools (Google's explicit-image removal, StopNCII.org, Meta's tools) that remove it even without a full DMCA notice.
Doing takedowns yourself is free but slow and repetitive; a service does it at scale and keeps re-filing on re-uploads.
Sending to the host's abuse@ or /dmca contact is stronger than the site's own on-page form, which is often ignored.
diy_takedown_steps: Collect evidence: copy the exact leak URL(s), a link to your original post (OnlyFans/Instagram) that proves it's yours, and today's date.
Find who to contact: look on the leak site for a 'DMCA', 'Abuse', 'Report' or 'Contact' link (often /dmca or in the footer) and note the email or form.

If there's no contact, find the host: run the domain through a whois / hosting lookup. If it sits behind Cloudflare, submit Cloudflare's abuse form at abuse.cloudflare.com — they forward your notice and reveal the real host so you can email them too.
Send a DMCA takedown notice (by email or the site's form) using the template below — include every required element or hosts can reject it.
Separately, ask Google to delist the URLs from search (see the Google section) so people stop finding them by your name.
Keep copies of everything. If the site ignores you after about 5-10 days, escalate to its hosting provider and domain registrar (both shown in the whois lookup).
Re-check every few weeks — leaks get re-uploaded, so re-send notices for any new copies.
dmca_notice_template:
Subject: DMCA Takedown Notice
To whom it may concern,
I am the copyright owner of the content being infringed. This is a formal notice under the DMCA (17 U.S.C. 512).
1. The original work: photos/videos I created and own (e.g. my OnlyFans/Instagram account: <your original link>).
2. The infringing material to be removed: <paste the leak URL(s)>.
3. My contact details: <name / email>.
4. I have a good-faith belief that this use is not authorized by me, my agent, or the law.
5. I state under penalty of perjury that this information is accurate and that I am the owner (or authorized to act for the owner) of the copyright.
6. Signature: <your full name>, <date>.
google_search_removal: Google removal is separate from the host: it hides the leak from search results even if a copy stays online.
For copyright: submit the infringing URLs through Google's DMCA / 'Remove Content' legal request form (search 'Google DMCA removal request').
For nude/sexual images posted without consent: use Google's dedicated 'remove personal explicit images' tool — it delists them without needing a DMCA notice.
You can report many URLs in one request; delisting usually takes a few days.

faq.q: Is it legal for me to get this removed?
faq.a: Yes. You own the copyright to your own photos and videos, so sites hosting them without your permission are infringing and you can demand removal.
No. Anyone can send a DMCA notice for their own content — it just has to be accurate and made in good faith.
Usually 24 hours to a couple of weeks, depending on the host and its country. Google delisting is often just a few days.

faq.q: The site is ignoring me — what now?
faq.a: Escalate: send the notice to the site's hosting provider and registrar (found via a whois lookup or Cloudflare's abuse form), and delist the URLs on Google in parallel.
Some get re-uploaded, so it's normal to re-check and re-file. Ongoing monitoring catches new copies as they appear.

faq.q: What about non-US or foreign sites?
faq.a: DMCA may not bind them, but their hosts usually still act on an abuse complaint, and Google delisting works no matter where the site is.

faq.q: Can I just do it myself?
faq.a: Yes, for free — it's mostly time and repetition. A paid service is worth it when there are many sites or constant re-uploads, since it handles everything for you.

faq.q: Is my content or report shared with anyone?
faq.a: No. Your report is private and password-protected, and your content is only used to document the takedown targets.
